title: When the Output Has to Hold Together
description: Three image tools judged by whether the result physically works: brick models that connect, furniture that cuts to a list, interfaces compared side by side.
content:
# When the Output Has to Hold Together

Most image generation is judged by how it looks. The three tools here are judged by whether the result works — whether the bricks connect, whether the parts fit on the sheet, whether the interface behaves.

That is a much harder bar, and it produces much more interesting software.

## Bricks that actually connect

[[link:/tools/2279|BricksChat]] turns an idea or a photo into a real brick model you can build. You describe something or drop in a picture, and it picks existing parts, borrows techniques from official sets, renders the model, and checks every version for real stud and pin connections, colliding parts and floating pieces.

The check is the product. Plenty of tools can generate a plausible-looking model; very few will tell you that two pieces intersect or that one is hovering. Connection checking is not a rendering problem, it is a graph problem: every part has ports, every port has a position in space, and a build is legal only if the ports line up and the parts do not occupy the same volume. A model that merely looks right can still be unbuildable, and the difference only shows up in your hands.

It also works the other way: photograph your shelf or pile of bricks and it designs with what you already own, which is a genuinely useful constraint that no general image model can express. Inventory is a harder input than a prompt, because the tool cannot invent a part it does not have — it has to route around the gap the way a person does.

Output is a 3D view, a parts list and instructions, downloadable for any LDraw-compatible building app. The LDraw export matters more than it sounds: it means the model is not trapped in the tool, and you can open it in the same software the hobby has used for twenty years. It is explicit that very large or unusual builds may still need a small fix by hand, which is the right kind of honesty for a generative tool.

## Furniture that cuts to a list

[[link:/tools/2280|Fabivo]] starts from a freehand sketch. Four rough strokes with a finger, pen or mouse become a parametric piece of furniture with sides, shelves, dividers, doors and drawers at real dimensions — and moving a shelf updates the related parts in one undoable edit.

Then the interesting part: a guillotine optimizer places those parts on your actual sheets, accounting for saw kerf, edge trim, grain direction and the priority you choose, and every sheet comes with a diagram and a numbered cut order a saw can follow. Assembly instructions come from the model itself: isometric diagrams, hardware, tools and one check per step.

It runs in the browser, works offline, needs no account, and is free. Exports cover GLB, DXF, PDF, SVG and CSV. It is not a CAD tool and does not pretend to be — it is the tool for the person who sketches on a napkin and then loses the plan in a spreadsheet.

## Interfaces compared, not admired

[[link:/tools/2281|UIPalooza]] is doing something no one else in this group attempts: testing whether AI models have a recognizable taste. Give the same brief to several models with different design skills, then compare the resulting interfaces side by side — desktop and mobile variants, the runtime and tokens behind each, and a published methodology.

Rows are models and columns group samples by skill variant, and clicking a preview opens the working artifact rather than a screenshot. That last detail matters: an interface that looks good in a still and breaks on hover is not evidence of anything. The sample sizes are small by design, and it is a lab rather than a design tool, but it is the only place here that treats design output as something to be measured.

## The bar that separates them

A general image model can produce a picture of a brick castle. It cannot produce one where the drawbridge hinges on a real part. It can produce a picture of a bookshelf; it cannot produce a cut list with 4.7 percent waste and a numbered order of passes.

[[link:/tools/2279|BricksChat]] and [[link:/tools/2280|Fabivo]] both sit on the far side of that line, and the reason is structural: they generate from a model of the object rather than a model of the image. The constraint is what makes the output usable.

[[link:/tools/2281|UIPalooza]] applies the same scepticism to a softer output. It does not ask whether an AI-designed interface is beautiful. It asks whether the same brief produces a recognizable house style, and then shows you the artifacts so you can decide.

If you are evaluating any generative tool this quarter, that is the question to steal: not how good is the output, but what would have to be true for the output to be wrong, and can the tool tell you.
tldr: BricksChat checks every brick model for real stud connections, Fabivo turns a sketch into a cut list with kerf and grain accounted for, and UIPalooza compares AI-generated interfaces rather than admiring them.
